planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into rich, well-drained soil in bright shade; most reliable as a protected woodland or shade-house plant in zones 9-11, though some growers report success with mulch protection in warmer zone 7b-8 pockets.

directions: Native to 4,000-6,000 foot elevations in Yunnan, Guangxi, and northern Indochina, this rhizomatous species gets its fan-begonia name from the way its pleated, fuzzy, palmately lobed leaves fold upward like a hand fan from a low, creeping rhizome. Because it comes from cool montane forest understory rather than lowland tropics, it tolerates brief cold somewhat better than most rhizomatous begonias. Give it bright shade, even moisture, and rich well-drained soil, and propagate readily from rhizome or leaf cuttings.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring into a chunky, fast-draining mix in dappled shade; too much sun scorches the puckered leaf surface, so grow as a terrarium or shade-house specimen outside zone 10-12.

directions: Collected from steep, shaded limestone slopes along small streams in the Mexican state of Oaxaca, this low creeping rhizomatous species is named for the blistered or pustulate texture of its deep velvety-green leaves, netted with pale silver veins. In cultivation it wants the same dappled, humid rainforest-understory light it gets in the wild, and benefits from a chunky, fast-draining mix that mimics the thin, rocky soils of its native habitat.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring and train up a moss pole or let cascade from a hanging basket in bright, filtered shade; protect from direct hot sun, which bleaches the glossy foliage.

directions: Unlike the rosette-forming begonias that dominate the genus, this Brazilian species is a true scandent climber, its succulent, flexible stems rooting at the nodes as they scramble up mossy trunks or trellises in the wild, bearing smooth, glossy, rounded-to-angular leaves. It produces loose clusters of small white flowers through late winter and benefits from extra humidity and airflow to avoid mildew on its soft stems.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into a sheltered, shaded spot through summer; needs frost-free protection through winter outside the warmest zones.

directions: A low, mat-forming Mexican species grown almost entirely for its textured, hairy, deep-green leaves splashed silver along the veins, a clump-forming groundcover rather than an upright specimen, rarely exceeding about a foot in height or spread. Small white flowers appear sparingly in winter, but the plant's real value is as dense, textural shade groundcover for a warm-climate woodland bed or large terrarium.

planting.note: Plant rhizome sections in spring into a chunky, well-drained mix in bright shade with even moisture.

directions: First discovered in 1967 near Ocozocoautla in Chiapas, Mexico, this rhizomatous species produces large, lobed, bright lime-green leaves with deeply set veins that give the surface a distinctive puffy, quilted look. It spreads vigorously by lateral rhizomes, quickly filling a wide shallow pot or shaded bed margin, and produces modest clusters of white flowers in late winter to early spring.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into a deeply shaded, moist woodland bed receiving only brief afternoon sun; genuinely rare in cultivation, so verify current nursery stock before planning around it.

directions: Ranging from Tibet across south-central China to Myanmar and Nagaland, this Himalayan and Chinese woodland saxifrage has kidney-shaped, many-lobed leaves and airy sprays of white flowers carried on reddish, hair-covered stems that give flowering clumps a soft pink haze. Treat it like a tougher relative of the already-present Saxifraga fortunei, giving it a deeply shaded, moist woodland spot.
